summary:
**BhuVyom: NASA-Powered Geospatial Intelligence Platform**

BhuVyom addresses the challenge of fragmented environmental data and disconnected tools that make understanding environmental change difficult. It brings multiple NASA Earth observation and climate datasets into one integrated platform, transforming complex scientific data into actionable insights.

Using datasets such as NASA POWER, MODIS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, SRTM and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, BhuVyom analyses temperature, precipitation, vegetation, land surface conditions and elevation. Its interconnected engines perform historical trend analysis, machine-learning-based predictions, long-term climate projections and environmental simulations. Users can explore how environmental conditions have changed, examine potential future scenarios and simulate how changes in land-surface conditions may affect runoff.

By combining data acquisition, scientific research, geospatial visualisation and predictive modelling in one platform, BhuVyom reduces the complexity of environmental analysis. Its goal is to make Earth science more accessible and support informed environmental planning, risk assessment and climate resilience.
details:
BhuVyom: NASA-Powered Environmental Intelligence

We built BhuVyom for the NASA Space Apps challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!". We wanted to understand how Bengaluru's environment is changing using NASA data, and to be honest about what that data can and can't tell us. BhuVyom pulls in NASA Earth observations and turns them into maps, tested trends, forecasts, climate projections and "what if" runoff simulations. Every result is labelled as observed, analysed, predicted, projected or simulated, so you always know what you're looking at.

What does the project do and how does it work?

The platform is built around five engines.

1. Getting and preparing the data

We pull real NASA data for the Bengaluru (BBMP) region:

  • SRTM elevation at 30 m.
  • MODIS MOD11A1 day and night land surface temperature.
  • MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (vegetation).
  • GPM IMERG daily rainfall.
  • NASA POWER monthly weather from 1981 to 2026, across 25 grid cells.
  • NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections.

Each dataset has its own resolution, units, quality flags and gaps, so we read the product documentation and handled each one properly instead of treating them as interchangeable. One example: MODIS's strictest quality filter threw out most of central Bengaluru, because built-up areas tend to get flagged. Rather than lose the city, we kept those pixels as a separate tier when their error was 2 K or less. Missing values stay missing. We never fill them with made-up numbers.

2. Finding trends and patterns

We used established statistical methods to tell real trends apart from noise:

  • Mann-Kendall tests to detect trends.
  • Sen's slope, with confidence intervals, to measure how big a trend is.
  • Pre-whitening to deal with autocorrelation.
  • Benjamini-Hochberg correction, so testing 25 cells at once doesn't produce false alarms.
  • Spearman correlation between surface temperature, vegetation and elevation.

Some of what we found:

  • From 1981 to 2025, 2 of the 25 cells warmed significantly, by about 0.15 °C per decade, both west of the city. The city's own cell warmed by about 0.10 °C per decade, but that isn't statistically significant (p = 0.17).
  • In the dry season (Jan-Mar 2024), central Bengaluru was 1-3 °C cooler at the surface than the bare land and farmland around it. We didn't expect that. Higher ground also tended to be cooler (ρ = -0.32).

3. Forecasts and climate projections

Short-term forecasts (1 to 12 months ahead)

We forecast monthly air temperature and rainfall using six candidate models, from simple baselines up to Ridge regression and gradient boosting. For each forecast horizon, the model that performs best on past data wins. A complex model is only picked if it clearly beats the simple average for that month.

We tested this the strict way. Models trained on 1981-2015, were chosen on 2017-2021, had their uncertainty ranges tuned on 2022-2025, and were tested once on 2026 data they had never seen. We also built in a two-month delay for data availability, so no model could peek at the future. We scored models on MAE, RMSE, bias and R², and checked that the 80% and 95% uncertainty ranges actually held up.

The results: temperature forecasts are 26% more accurate than the monthly average one month ahead and 13% two months ahead, and the advantage fades after about four months. Rainfall forecasts don't beat the average at all, so BhuVyom tells you that and shows the average instead. Every experiment is saved in an append-only, checksummed log, so old results can't be quietly overwritten.

Long-term projections

We use NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 data to show how Bengaluru's climate could change under three emissions scenarios: SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Following IPCC practice, we compare each period (around 2030, 2050, 2070 and 2100) with a 1995-2014 baseline. We show the median across climate models along with their full range. The indicators are average temperature, hot days (35 °C or above), annual rainfall, heavy-rain days (64.5 mm or more, the IMD threshold), humidity and wind speed. These are published climate-model results, kept separate from our own forecasts.

4. Runoff simulation

What happens to rainwater when more of the city gets paved over? We used the USDA SCS Curve Number method on real daily GPM rainfall to compare runoff today with a scenario that has more concrete. Soil type and other key settings are uncertain, so we run six variations and show the range of results. The model covers surface runoff only. It doesn't model drains, lakes or flooding, and we haven't been able to check it against river-flow measurements.

5. Visualisation

All of this lives in an interactive web app with five pages: Home, an Explorer map, a Simulation Lab, Future Earth and a forecast dashboard. There's also a mobile app built with Expo (React Native). You can animate data over time, export CSVs, and press Shift+I to open the Scientific Inspector, which shows the equations, parameters and processing steps behind any number.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

BhuVyom can help planners, researchers, students and anyone curious about the city to:

  • See which warming trends are real and which are just noise.
  • Understand why some parts of the city run hotter than others.
  • Get short-term temperature outlooks, including how reliable they are.
  • Compare Bengaluru's future climate under different emissions scenarios.
  • Explore how paving over land changes runoff from real rainfall.

We hope it supports better decisions in urban planning, water management, farming and climate adaptation. Because every number can be traced back to its source and method, you can check it before you act on it.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, KaTeX.
  • Mobile: Expo / React Native.
  • Maps and charts: MapLibre GL, deck.gl, Recharts, d3-scale, Three.js.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, Pydantic.
  • Scientific computing: NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, xarray, netCDF4, h5py.
  • Machine learning: scikit-learn.
  • Geospatial: Rasterio, Shapely, PyProj.
  • Data and testing: Supabase (PostgreSQL), JSON/JSONL experiment logs, GitHub Actions for scheduled data updates, pytest (60 tests).
  • Data sources: NASA Earthdata, NASA POWER, MODIS, GPM IMERG, SRTM, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6.

BhuVyom is entirely software and runs on ordinary computers.

How is the project creative, and what factors did the team consider?

Most satellite dashboards stop at showing data on a map. We wanted to go further and ask what the data can actually support. That meant reading research papers and NASA documentation, writing down each method's equations, assumptions and limits, and then turning them into code we could test.

A few decisions shaped the whole project:

  • We kept observations, analysis, forecasts, projections and simulations clearly separate, because each one rests on different assumptions and comes with different uncertainty.
  • BhuVyom refuses requests the science can't support. For example, it won't run the runoff model on monthly forecast averages, and it won't predict temperature street by street when the source data covers about 50 km.
  • We report results that didn't pan out too, such as city warming that isn't statistically significant and rainfall forecasts with no skill.

Along the way we had to think about resolution, data quality, missing data, autocorrelation, testing many cells at once, data leakage, uncertainty, reproducibility and scale.

What we're proudest of is bringing satellite data, statistics, machine learning, climate projections and hydrology together in one place, without hiding the limits of any of them.
